utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic, and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis, and the case manager Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have appearances for the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President; good morning Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel, and Alexis Demirdjian, my legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused and everyone else present. We have a witness scheduled for today as we said yesterday, but before we call the witness into the courtroom, I'd like to ask the Defence whether they have managed to prepare their list of documents to be tendered into evidence through the witness we heard yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Defence counsel has prepared its list, and as I explained yesterday, we would like to tender into evidence the academic and other documents which form the basis for this witness's testimony, whereas the documents about the facts and the parties in the conflict will be tendered through witnesses who are familiar with these documents or the events related in the documents. According to the list that we provided yesterday and with references of the sources used by Mr. Sehic, we suggest that annex A the following documents be admitted into evidence. In our list of documents they have the following numbers, 1601, 0350, 0351, 0362, 0354, 0356, 0353. From Annex C, we would like to tender into evidence documents 1598, 1590, and 0378. Mr. President, since we have copies for everyone, could the usher distribute copies of the list of documents so that everyone can follow more easily. From Annex C, we would like to tender into evidence the following documents: 0385 and 0510. From Annex E, we would like to tender into evidence one document. The number in our list of this document is 1599. From Annex G, we would like to tender two documents into evidence, and they have the numbers 1398 and 1004 in our list of documents. We would also suggest that documents 1623, 1624, 1625, 1626, and 1627 be admitted into evidence. These are documents from the Zenica Red Cross. And in part of his report, Dr. Sehic used these documents. He based his analysis on these documents in the part that refers to ethnic cleansing. We also suggest that the following documents be admitted into evidence: Documents from the file of Dr. Sehic, 0353, 0357, 0358, 0359, 0363, 1589. We also suggest that the expert report of Dr. Sehic be admitted into evidence as well as the set of maps from 1 to 17, maps that were made by this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this list of documents. I would like to ask the Prosecution whether they have any comments to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objections nor comments to make. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges will discuss the matter, and we will inform you either today or on Thursday of our decision. In the meantime, the registrar will have sufficient time to prepare definitive exhibit numbers. We'll now call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Could you tell me whether you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you, and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You've been called here as a witness for the Defence to testify about the events that took place in 1993. Before I ask you to read out the solemn declaration, I would like you to tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ribo Sulejman. I was born on the 19th of February, 1953, in Skomorje, Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Are you currently employed? What is your current professional status?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I work in the ministry of education, science, culture and sport in the Central Bosnia canton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what position do you hold there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work as a professional official, professional advisor for educational matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, 1993, did you hold a position of any kind and, if so, could you tell me what sort of position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At the time, I didn't have a position of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is my first time as a witness before such a court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence who will commence your examination-in-chief, I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that we will follow here, because as you have said, this is the first time you have appeared as a witness before a court. You have just taken the solemn declaration. You have said you will speak the truth and nothing but the truth. This means that you will not give false testimony, because false testimony is an offence which is punishable, and a prison sentence could be given for false testimony. When responding to questions, in certain cases a witness might provide the Judges with information that could be used in the subsequent Prosecution against that witness, but you should be aware of the fact that in such exceptional cases, you have a form of immunity. So you can feel completely free to answer questions, because you risk nothing unless you give false testimony. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel for one of the accused, and then perhaps you will have to answer put to you by the Defence team for the other accused. Try to provide precise answers, because we have no written statement. The procedure we follow here is an oral procedure. It's important for the Judges to understand what you say, so try to form your answers in the clearest possible way. If you don't understand a question, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it to make sure that you do understand the question. Once Defence counsel has concluded its examination-in-chief, you will have to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. The Prosecution is to your right. This is what we call the cross-examination, the purpose of which is to verify the credibility of your statements and also to clarify some of the answers you provided in the course of the examination-in-chief. After this procedural stage, Defence counsel may re-examine you. The three Judges before you may also ask you questions at any point in time. As a rule, the Judges ask questions either to clarify the answers that a witness provided or to fill in any gaps. According to the rules followed when the Judges asked questions -- after the Judges have asked questions, the other parties, Prosecution and Defence, may ask you additional questions. Roughly speaking, this is how we will be proceeding here today. The hearing will be adjourned at 1.45 at the latest. For technical reasons, there will be two breaks. Each break will last half an hour, and will give the opportunity to have a rest and will give the technicians the possibility of dealing with technical matters. If you encounter any difficulties, please inform us of the fact. Defence counsel may now take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ribo.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard what the president of the Trial Chamber said, but I would like to ask you to pay attention to the following: We speak the same language, and you might immediately reply to my answers, but since what we are saying is being interpreted, in order to make sure that the Chamber and my colleagues in the courtroom can follow what is being said, I would be grateful if you could wait after I've asked you my question so that it can be interpreted, and only then answer the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is your nationality, and what citizenship do you have?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak, and I'm a citizen of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you live now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I live in Travnik now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you on the 6th of April, 1992, when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina broke out?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: On the 6th of April, 1992, which is when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina officially began, I was in the Republic of Croatia. I have two brothers near the town of Nasice in Croatia. They have lived there since about 1981 or 1982, and at the time I was staying with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, did you ever return to Bosnia and Herzegovina and, if so, where did you return to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I returned to Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 25th of May, 1992. I returned to my place of birth, and naturally, I returned to my own municipality, to the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me a little about your educational background. What is your profession, and where were you educated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I'm a professor of geography. I finished the mathematics at the university in Sarajevo in 1977. After graduation, I mostly worked in schools, mostly in the Mehurici primary school where I worked for about 11 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, did you serve in the army before the war and, if so, which army did you serve in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I did my military service in the JNA from 1978 to 1979.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you obtain a rank in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was an ordinary private.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which service, which branch of the army were you in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I was in the artillery, howitzer artillery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you left the JNA, were you given a wartime assignment, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: After leaving the JNA, I was given a wartime assignment in the local commune, in the Territorial Defence of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We said that you returned from the Republic of Croatia towards the end of May. Did you at any point in time join any armed formations, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: When I returned from Croatia, I reported to the Travnik Territorial Defence Staff. I told them that I had been in the artillery. It was agreed that I and a group of men from the area of my place of birth should form a platoon, an artillery platoon, because there was a 105-millimetre howitzer in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, when you arrived in Travnik in the Territorial Defence staff, that is to say when you arrived in the area you lived in, were you able to observe what sort of situation the Territorial Defence was in -- or, rather, were you able to see how it had been organised or how it was equipped for the combat activities that about already underway?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: My impression was that the Territorial Defence in the Travnik area was organised on the whole in local communes. These were Territorial Defence staffs of the local communes. One was also able to observe that most of the men were Bosniaks, because one could already see that the Croatian population had already joined the HVO. So these were some of the impressions I gained when I arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the members of the Territorial Defence have any weapons, and if so, what kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The impression they gave was that they had very few weapons, and especially in the area where I lived, people had their own weapons, for example, hunting weapons. And there were some automatic weapons, too, but very few. As far as other equipment is concerned, I think there was almost no equipment on the whole. As far as I could observe, people who were going to positions used their own weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you were assigned a task in the Municipal Staff, and you were to form a platoon to man the howitzer. Were you able to form a crew capable of using that howitzer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Towards the end of May, we received an order from the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff according to which we were to place the weapon at a position called Kaurske Ravni. We were first to find at least eight to ten men who had been in artillery units in the former JNA. This was necessary for us to be able to use the howitzer. We had seven or eight such men, so at the very beginning, we were able to use that weapon, but since the same men cannot be permanently present at the position, we started training another crew. And this is what we did in the first few months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you just said that you were ordered to place the howitzer at Kaurske Ravni. Could you tell us where Kaurske Ravni is located, and which positions was your weapon directed at so to speak?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, Kaurske Ravni is on the north-eastern side of the Vlasic -- on Mt. Vlasic's slopes. It's about an hour or an hour and a half from Mehurici if you go on foot. Our task was to engage on that axis in the direction of the Serbian forces, that is to say the peripheral areas of Travnik municipality, Kotor Varos and Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, at any point in time towards the end of 1992, were there any changes in the in the organisation of the Territorial Defence or in the organisation of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, the first brigades were established in our area. The 312th Motorised Brigade was established. Its base was in Travnik. Also the 306th Brigade was established. Its base was in the Bila region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you become a member of any of the brigades, and what position did you hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Our howitzer was given to the 312th Motorised Brigade, although we were in a certain way in a different area. The howitzer was necessary to support the units on that axis in the Travnik municipality. We got on the strength of the 312th Motorised Brigade. Otherwise, we were part of the unit that was initially called a Mixed Artillery Division, although according to the number of pieces, men, and logistics, it could not have been a division. It was more of a platoon that we served in with our howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you've told us that at the beginning there was seven of us -- of you and that after that you started training a certain number of men and that you managed to train these people. Tell me, who was responsible for the training of these people who were supposed to be using the howitzer together with you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The training was organised by our people who had served in the JNA, in the artillery of the JNA, and who attended a number of military manoeuvres in the 80s and the 90s, and it is in this way that we were able to train men and replenish our platoon. And in the space of some two months or so, we had two completely trained crews.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, when you were not on the position on Mt. Vlasic, where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. were you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I mostly stayed at home. My house is two kilometres away from Mehurici, and this is where I mostly stayed. From time to time I would go to Travnik, of course, although I must say that already at that time the movement of people was in a certain way restricted. There were a lot of checkpoints on the roads, so this hampered any normal movement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what is the name of your village where you resided at the time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Luka Zagredja is the name of my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your brigade in that area or anywhere else, did it have barracks where troops were billeted?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: No, our brigade did not have any barracks. At the time, the barracks housed the so-called 7th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade that was mostly replenished from the Bila region, the 306th Brigade, did it have its barracks where the troops of the 306th Brigade were accommodated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: No. The 306th Brigade did not have its barracks. The troops would go home once they did not have to be around the positions. So they spent their free time at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that your village is some two kilometres away from the village of Mehurici. Where did you have to go from your village in order to reach the positions where your howitzer was? What was your usual route?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: There were two roads that we normally used, the two of them being very close to each other. When we went on foot, we would go through Zagredja, and we would climb to Kaurske Ravni. It took us about an hour and a half to two hours. The second road was via Mehurici, and then we would take a dirt road through Orahovo and further on to the mountain, to Kaurske Ravni where we were manning the positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the end of May 1992, when you arrived in the Bila valley and where you stayed in 1992 and 1993, did you notice at any point in time that some foreigners arrived in the Bila valley, people who were not from the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime at the beginning of summer, already at a certain point in time we noticed some people who had arrived in Mehurici. We could clearly see that those were foreigners, that those were of foreign origin. They moved around on their own. They did not have many contacts with the locals. And we could not obtain any information as to where they had come from, who they were, why they had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you assume where they came from judging by their speech or their appearance?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: It was not very difficult to tell for some individuals. They spoke various languages, but we could recognise the Arabic. But some of them also spoke English and French.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the autumn of 1992 and later on, did you notice their clothes, how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: At the beginning and, actually, for a somewhat longer period of time, they mostly wore traditional clothes such as are worn in the Arabic world. Truth be told, some started wearing uniforms after a certain period of time, but very often they would have the typical clothes of the Arabic world worn over the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, what did you call these people? Did there come a time when a name started being used for these foreigners who had arrived in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: At the beginning, in the summer and autumn of 1992, we would simply call them Arabs, foreigners. Later on, all of a sudden, the term "Mujahedin" started being used, and I heard from the people who had contacts with them that they wanted and asked to be called the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you have just told us that you teach geography, that this is your vocation. Before the war, did you know anything about the Mujahedin in the former Yugoslavia and the former Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was anything known about this type of people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I personally never heard or knew anything about the Mujahedin. I can only say that while I was reading about the war in Afghanistan, I came across this term, but it never occurred to me to dwell upon this term. This term became somewhat more topical at the moment when these people appeared in our village and started using this name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, when you go back to that period of time, what did you think? Why would Travnik and Mt. Vlasic be interesting for these people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I can't say with any degree of certainty. My assumption is that Travnik was a vizir town, the seat of nobility during the Turkish times, and this lasted for 150 years. Maybe this was the fact that they found attractive and interesting. Furthermore, I could say that Travnik, as a town, has a number of mosques, which is another reason why these people may have appeared in the region. At the same time, the Bila region had a majority Muslim population, which may have been another reason for them to choose this region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In the autumn of 1992, were you aware of the place where these foreigners stayed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion when I left the positions, I noticed in -- noticed them entering the school in Mehurici and taking the uppermost floor of the school. This is where they were accommodated. In that village, the school was no longer used, and that's where they found their accommodation. The staff of the Territorial Defence, that is of the Mehurici detachment, was also billeted in the school, on the ground floor and on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, is that the same school where you used to teach for 11 years?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same school. And truth be told, I found it very strange that these people were accommodated in the school. I even raised this as an issue, but the times were what they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many people were there approximately, and was their number constant? Did it change?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I can just share my impressions with you. It was very difficult to estimate the exact number of these people at any given point in time. The fact is that at the beginning, there were -- there's not so many of them, but they moved around all the time, and they mostly moved in the vehicles that they owned. It was really very difficult to come up with any estimate or conclusion as to their approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, as a teacher, you must have known a lot of people in the area. It is not fair for me to assume that. However, bearing in mind your position and your profession, did you know the population of the surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The mere fact that I was born in the area and that I worked there for a long time must tell you that I knew people from these villages because I taught their children. I mostly knew these people and their mentality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time did you observe or were you informed or did you see yourself that these foreigners were trying to recruit some of the local population to their ranks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: After some month or two months of their permanent stay in Mehurici, we could notice that some locals were approaching them and spending time with them. There was some training going on. Since I used to teach these young lads, I wanted to find out what their motive was given the fact that we already had our Territorial Defence. I wanted to know why they decided to approach the foreigners whom they didn't know. Most of them told me that the reason was that they were offered uniforms, weapons. They were told that once they completed their training that they would get uniforms and weapons. At the time, as I've already told you, the population did not have any means to obtain either uniform or weapon. And you also have to be aware of the poverty of a large number of families in that area. So in many of these young lads, this was another motive for approaching these foreigners. Truth be told, I noticed that many of these young men, after their training, after having been given what they desired, returned to their detachment, the Mehurici detachment. However, a certain number of young lads remained with the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, could you please tell us if these foreigners remained on the top floor of this school or if at some point they went to a different location.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Having in mind the fact that they -- by their religion they were committed in a way that was not quite appropriate to our area. The way they presented Islam did not fit in in every way. Also, the people from the detachment who were billeted there did not practice all the religious precepts. They noticed that, and it was obvious that they were bothered by this, and they simply were looking for a different location so that they would not be there together with the members of the TO detachment. At this point, I don't know exactly what, but I know that after two or three months, there was a settlement next to Mehurici which was once populated by Serbs who, by that time, had already left except for one or two people. So they went into that settlement and proclaimed it their camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to go freely into that camp, and was it secured by them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, the camp, I really don't know. I didn't have the opportunity to go there, but I know that very few had that opportunity. The only people who could go there were people that had gained some trust there. Just normal regular people and soldiers were not able to go there. Since they guarded it by day and night, the camp was quite separate. And I even know that one road that existed. It was a pedestrian path. In regard of that path, they told the villagers of the Poljanica village not to use that path but to take a different route.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, do you think that the presence of these foreigners created certain problems amongst the local population which did not respond to their call to join them?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: There were certain disagreements, even some minor incidents with them. First of all because people did not join them and did not practice the religion in the way that they did. So they felt that we were in some way Muslims of lesser worth because we were not practising our religion in the way that they were doing. Especially on market days, on the day when people from that region come down in larger numbers to the market day. On such days, the younger people, especially women and girls, did not change the way they dressed. For the most part, they behaved the way they did before. But on many occasions, what would happen was that they would approach these women and girls in an arrogant way, pull their hair, threaten them, take out their weapons. I was not present on any such occasion, but when I took some time off from my position, people would say that -- would tell me that there had been certain situations which were quite delicate and that could have resulted in incidents. And that is also another reason why they had pulled out from the school and had gone to this camp, so that they would be separate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, I wanted to ask you another thing. In this Biljani valley area, besides the units of the units of Bosnia-Herzegovina, you said you were from the 312th. There was also the 306th unit there. Could you please tell us whether the population from that area was mobilised into some other brigades which were not based in the Biljani valley?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: People were mobilised, those who were expelled from the northern part of the Travnik municipality, from the area of Kravulja, with the fall of the town of Jajce and the population having moved out of there, had left the town to go to the settlement of Karaula. That population, out of fear, also pulled out together with the inhabitants of Jajce to other parts of the Travnik municipality, because it was well known that this line was established in the town of Turbe. So a large number of this population from the area of Karaula, which comprises some 15 villages, lived part in the Biljani Dolina. So as they were moving out, they found accommodation in that area or in Zenica or in Vitez. So there were some. But they still belonged to their home unit, to the 312th Brigade in Travnik. So there were some cases in times when they were going for their positions that they would go on to Travnik, and they would go further on to Travnik where their positions were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members of some detachments from the Biljani valley agreed to be members of some other unit and not the 306th unit?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: As I said, for the most part from those bordering or outlying parts of the Travnik municipality such as Karaula, all the members returned to the 312th. We also had examples from Vitez. A certain number of people also returned there for their service. They did not wish to switch from their home unit. We also have the outlying Travnik municipalities such as Kotor Varos, Skender Vakuf, Jajce. They also, although they lived in the Biljani region, would go to serve in these other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me now, besides units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, regardless of whether we're talking about the 312th, 306th, or some other unit, were there other military units in the Biljani valley area?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I will tell you briefly. Since the Biljani valley is very specific in its distribution of settlements which were inhabited by Croats, Bosniaks, it's also true that there were few Serbs in that area. It was clear since the members of the Croat ethnicity for the most part did not want to serve in the Territorial Defence detachments, in that area, thus in places where the Croats had a majority, the HVO was formed. In that area, there was a pronounced presence of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, in the spring of 1993, until June, which combat operations -- which combat formations were controlling the main roads towards Travnik and Zenica in the Biljani region?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: In view of the position, I spoke a little bit earlier about how those settlements were distributed. It looked like a chequerboard or we could use some other example. But from the Biljani Dolina, from Travnik Mehurici, or Han Bila, in order to reach Travnik you had to pass through at least five, six, or seven settlements where the Croats had a majority. A similar situation was in the direction of Zenica whether we're talking about the only road we had to Zenica via Nako. That whole area comprises seven or eight settlements which are mostly inhabited by Croats. So there were already incidents of checkpoints being set up and of more difficult movements. At certain points there was even a total break. So in a way, as time went on, the situation constantly worsened, and at certain points it was impossible to leave the Biljani area to go to Travnik or to the other side, to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would now like to ask the usher to show the witness a document. This is the only document that I would like to present to the witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, could you please tell us, you can see at the top of this document the name of the brigade. Is this a brigade that you belonged to as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. That's the 312th Motorised Brigade to which I belonged to originally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at page 2. There is a signature there. Do you know the person of this name, and do you know if this person was in the brigade and what were their duties?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Ivan Nedoklan is a person that I know. I know him, living in that area. I have known him since 1975 or so. He was from the beginning until the end and still today a member of this brigade, and he was a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now please look at the content of this document, and then when you read the document, could you please tell me whether you as a soldier of the 312th Brigade saw things happening that are mentioned in this document. Have you looked at the document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I have. This document, according to what I know, more or less reflects the situation as it was in that period, in January 1993, in this area. I would just like to note that the situation with the HVO forces, in particular the cooperation, worsened from the first clash in the region of Novi Travnik, and then this situation moved on to or included Travnik or spread to Travnik. So I think there is no need to go paragraph by paragraph in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, we don't do that, but what I wanted to know was that whether you as a soldier in the Bila valley could sense this worsening of relations with the HVO, and you gave us the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where the lines of the HVO were in the Bila valley?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, the Defence lines of the HVO were mostly in those parts of settlements or the land which belonged to the Croats. Even though it was deep inside the defence area in relation to the front line towards the Serb forces, they dug in and had their lines. I know this very well. We as an artillery unit, which by the nature of things is in the rear, they were, however, in the rear of us. For example, they were a few kilometres behind us as the crow flies. And all this seemed to indicate that something was not quite right. This is something that I noticed right away, and of course this bothered us and gave rise to some doubts and insecurity because somebody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. was digging in behind our back and setting up some kind of line of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to talk about your personal knowledge about a specific event. Could you please tell us if you know where the village of Miletici is?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I know where the village of Miletici is. It is very close to my house where I live, the Luka that I mentioned before. It's about some 400 or 500 metres. The village of Miletici is in a sort of clearing on one side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where were you on the 24th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: On the 24th of April, 1993, I was at the position in my unit at Kaurske Ravni that has already been mentioned. In the afternoon on that day, it was necessary for me to go down to my house and to Mehurici because of messages that I had received from a unit in Travnik. It was about 1700 hours when I went down to Mehurici, and on my way there I noticed a lot of people who were moving around in a confused manner. When I entered this settlement, I saw a group of women crying, and I also noticed some young men standing nearby. Two of them approached me. I asked them about what was happening there. I asked them why one of the women was crying. They said that about five minutes ago, the Mujahedin had taken her husband away. Her husband's name was Alija Delalic. They had taken him to a camp. At that point in time, I noticed that notorious white Toyota that was returning over the bridge from the camp and continued in the direction of the school. They didn't linger there for long, perhaps two, three, or four minutes. They returned soon afterwards, and we saw that they were taking away another man who had been the secretary of the school for a long time. He had a flat near the school in which he lived with his family, and they took him to the camp too. I was confused and wondered about what I should do. The first thing I did was go to the commander of the battalion called the Sipraski Battalion because most of the men were from Siprage in Kotor Varos municipality, but there were also men from other neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you set off in the direction of the battalion command. Who did you find in the command when you went there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I found a man whose name was Mehmed Musanovic there. He was born in Skender Vakuf, and he was deputy commander of the battalion. I asked him whether he knew about what was happening. He said that he was also surprised and that he didn't understand what was going on. He was a man from Knezevo. Since part of the command was absent - they were somewhere at the positions - asked me to try and establish contact with the battalion commander or someone from the brigade command, because it was certainly time to do something, and there hadn't been any similar situations that might provoke problems and have serious consequences.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo. You said that you found this member of the 1st Battalion there. Can you tell me where the troops were, where the army was?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, it was absent. On the whole, the troops were at the positions. There was a conflict of some kind at the peripheral part of the municipality of Vitez. So that's where the troops were.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you told that member of the battalion that the commander should be called, did you subsequently find out anything else about the movement of the Mujahedin at that point in time? Did anyone inform you of their movement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, while I spoke to Mehmed, the man I have mentioned, there were people who were passing through, because it was quite surprising. The men wanted to obtain information at the command. They wanted to find out about what was happening. So people would appear there, and I know that at one point someone said that many Mujahedin had left Mehurici in vehicles, and they said they assumed or, rather, they said that someone had already found out that they had set off in the direction of the village of Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the information that you had, Mr. Ribo, do you know whether this soldier who was on duty contacted his commander and informed him of the situation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I can say that Mehmed Musanovic really did react immediately. He found a few men there, and he sent them in the direction of the unit's location, in a vehicle. I was there when he wrote something for the commander, but I also heard him say that if he couldn't -- if Fazlic couldn't come, the commander of the 1st Battalion should come, Mirza Lubenovic. Those what I heard him tell these two men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were trying to establish contact with someone from the battalion command or someone who might be able to come to the -- might be able to go to the school, to the command, did you find out anything else about these Mujahedin, and at any point in time did they appear in the village?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, time passes by very rapidly in such situations, more rapidly than usual. Around dusk, quite a few people had gathered in that common room or in what used to be the common room, but it was the command at the time. People spoke about various things, and it was said at one point that the Mujahedin were passing through Mehurici, and they were leading a column of people who had been tied up. They had almost crossed the bridge and turned off in the direction of the camp when we saw that they had done something. Since they had tied these people up and taken them to the camp, they had done something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this soldier Mehmed, and yourself and the people you sent to inform the commander, were there members of the BH army in the village itself who you could have engaged to provide assistance?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, at one point we were joined by a young man whose name was Suljic Dervis. He told me that his father had been taken away with the imprisoned people. And his father's brother, his uncle, and his father's uncle, an elderly man. So these were Bosniaks who lived in Donji Miletici who were also tied up and taken to that camp. That's what I found out there. And I saw that Suljic was very depressed. He was shaking. He seemed like a young man who was lost. We tried to soothe him; we said everything would be fine. We sent people to the command to see what should be done in such a situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, did you find out from those people that perhaps someone from among the civilian population had tried to resist those Mujahedin or at least ask them about what they were doing? And how did this affair end?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, at one point immediately after this column had been taken away in the direction of the camp, two young men approached me. They were neighbours of mine. One of them whose name was Meho Poparic, told me that he met the column of those local people at the entrance to the village of Mehurici, the column of the people being taken towards the camp. He tried to approach them and asked them why they had tied these people up and why they were taking them away. Mujahedin approached him and hit him with his rifle butt, and he fell into a ditch as a result of the blow.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation that you and the local people were in, did anyone from the battalion command appear at any point in time? And what did you decide to do or, rather, to attempt to do?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I must say that before anyone arrived from the battalion, there were quite a few people who lived there, and they wondered about what should be done in a reasonable, in a rational way. It was my impression that it was necessary to try and attempt to try to liberate the people as soon as possible. It was necessary to try to get them released, because we assumed that these people were perhaps not armed. We thought that they were probably not a threat, which is what the Mujahedin claimed, because these were people who lived there and we knew them. At about 7.00 or half past seven in the meaning, Mirza Lubenovic, the battalion commander, arrived. Naturally, as the commander, he took over the key role in attempting to find a solution to the problem, or, rather, in attempting to get the people from the camp released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone try to establish contact of any kind with those Mujahedin from that camp, and did anyone ever engage in negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, naturally -- first of all, the problem was that the problem couldn't be solved without their presence. We could take decisions of various kinds, but without the presence of their leading men, the problem couldn't be solved. Someone had an idea. At that time they had kept two rooms in the school, on the floor that they had occupied, and someone called Ramadan seemed to be logistics man for the Mujahedin. That's the impression we had. He always moved around independently. So someone thought of this man, and one went up there and called him. In about half an hour's time, he came down and said that he had no authority to discuss this matter since it was purely military matter and only the battalion commander could -- the only thing the battalion commander could do was try and establish contact with the main figure in the camp, Abu Haris. They said that he was from Libya, and they called him "Doctor." It seems that he had completed medical school. The commander sent some of his men to the camp, but they returned. He had refused to get involved in negotiations of any kind. Later on, perhaps because Lubenovic had insisted, Ramadan went up there with representatives from the battalion. We then found out that Abu Haris would come. He didn't say when, but he said he would come. And he did come at about half past nine in the evening, escorted by two or three armed men. They had their rifles at the ready. So at about half past nine, these negotiations started, negotiations to get these people released. We believed that these people were innocent and that it was not necessary for them to be kept in the camp. And if any action had to be taken against them, the army was there. And I must say that at that time in the Zagradje school, there was a platoon, a BH army platoon, that could assume the duty of guarding these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that negotiations had started. Do you know what the results of the negotiations were or, rather, do you know who the first person released was, and when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, towards the end of the negotiations, I found out that at about 10.00, these three Bosniaks were released, three Bosniaks who had been taken up there together with the Croats from the village of Miletici. I found out that they had been freed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: They were set free.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you continue to negotiate in order to release the other villagers of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course, we continued. We insisted that people should be released, that people should not stay in the camp over the night. I must say that the situation was as follows: Some kilometre or kilometre and a half away from Mehurici there was an HVO line from which fire was opened constantly. I spoke to the negotiators, to the representatives of the Mujahedin, and very simply we were afraid that there would be shooting and some of the Mujahedin might be wounded or killed. And this would lead to a tragedy, in our view. And that in that case, the Mujahedin would retaliate and kill a dozen or more people in the camp, of the prisoners. So we insisted that the negotiations should be brought to an end and that the people should be released.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, did you manage to convince these people from the camp, the Mujahedin, that they should release your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: These negotiations lasted until 11.00 in the evening, and Abu Haris had a lot of demands and requests. First of all, he wanted guarantees that these people would not flee. It was already dark. There was a forest very close. He wanted to know where they would be taken and accommodated. Obviously in all that, we had suggestions. My personal suggestion was that they -- these people should be accommodated in my house and in the houses of my neighbours and that we would guarantee the safety of these people. And we also guaranteed that none of them would flee. Having heard this suggestion, Abu Haris consulted his men and accepted our suggestion. Around half past eleven, the negotiations were completed. However, there was an additional problem, and the problem was how to transport these people up to those houses. It was dark. There were mountains on both sides. There was a bus there that was used for the transportation of the BiH army units. The driver was also there. So we said that the driver should bring the bus all the way to the camp, leaving only a distance of some ten metres between the bus and the detainees, and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have some ten or so questions for this witness. Maybe this is a good time for a break, and I would like to continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is time for the break. We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We resume our session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, before the break, you told us that finally you managed to convince the Mujahedin to release your neighbours, that you found a bus that would transport them from Mehurici. Where did you go? Where did you accommodate these people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: When these people were released from that building where they were accommodated and when they got on the bus, we drove off to Luka where my house is. As had been agreed, most of the people were accommodated in my house, on the ground floor, and seven or eight of them were accommodated in the three neighbouring houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the situation of these people, did the battalion commander offer them any additional assistance?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: At the end of our negotiations, it was said that a doctor would accompany us, and the doctor was there with us from the moment these people were released, and he stayed with them throughout the night. He was in my house most of the time, but from time to time he would also pay a visit to the neighbouring houses where some of the people from Miletici were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened on the following day and a few days thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: On the following day, on the 25th of April, very early in the morning I was told that I had to go to the position. I went there, and once my mission was accomplished, around noon of that day I returned via the village of Mehurici, and I got to my house. There I found these people on the road leading up to their village. It was a very nice day. I also noticed a few vehicles, a few UNPROFOR vehicles. I learned from the people who were present there that in the village up there, the mixed commission composed of members of the army and the HVO was there. They were carrying out a on-site inspection. Some ten or 15 minutes later, they appeared accompanied by an UNPROFOR vehicle. They addressed the people who were gathered in front of my house, and I recognised Mr. Dzemal Merdan, who represented the BH army, and I also recognised Mr. Nakic, who represented the HVO. In the conversation that we had with them, Merdan and Nakic asked the people whether they wished to stay in the village or, alternatively, whether they wanted to leave the village. Most of the people said that they wished to leave after the inspection was finished. A certain number, however, decided that they wanted to stay. They believed that they were safe there and that they trusted the BH army to protect them and to safeguard them. In the meantime, I learned from some of the young men that that evening when people were taken away, that four people stayed in the village and that they were killed. So at the end of the day, there were five dead bodies there because one of them had already been killed before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who buried these people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: These people were taken away on the 27th of April, an UNHCR vehicle took them to Nova Bila, and I really don't know where they were buried and what happened to the bodies after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The neighbours who said that they wanted to stay, did any of the members of the BH army get the task to secure them, or did they go to the village on their own?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The people who decided to stay in the village were promised that the platoon, which was present at all times in the Zagradje school, would provide security to the Miletici settlement and that they shouldn't fear for their safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, during the negotiations in which you yourself took part in the attempt to liberate your neighbours, did you, as a soldier, or the battalion commander who arrived subsequently, did you -- were you in a position to issue any orders to these foreigners? Were you under the impression that any sort of order could have been given to these foreigners?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The mere fact that we invested so much time and effort to reach the person in charge shows that there could have been no cooperation with them, let alone us issuing orders to them. They were independent in what they were doing, and it was impossible to cooperate with them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ribo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't have any Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team, do you have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We do have a few questions in order to clarify some of the answers that have been provided by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ribo, when you mentioned the 24th of April, 1993, and the events in Miletici, on that day, in the afternoon, you returned from the position; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And then you noticed that something was already going on. You were provided with the information that Mr. Delalic had been taken away, as well as Mr. Obradovic. Then you went to the command of the 1st Battalion. When you said the 1st Battalion, you meant the 306th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, when you mentioned the 1st Battalion on page 24, 25, 26 of today's LiveNote, you meant the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mehmed Musanovic whom you've mentioned --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: -- he was the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: During the events and the negotiations with the Mujahedin and the events that you saw and witnessed, you did not notice any of the officers or members of the 7th Brigade on that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, that is corrected. I did not notice any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We have no further questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleague Mr. Neuner, we represent the Prosecution in this case, and we're going to be asking you some questions until the next technical break. I want to start by saying that it is not my intention in any way to confuse you, so that if you don't understand any of my questions, I would kindly ask you to tell me that, and I will either rephrase or repeat the question so that you fully understand it before you answer.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just start by asking you some questions so that I fully understand your testimony. From the beginning of when the 312th Motorised Brigade was formed until the end of 1993, did you remain with that brigade throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. From the very establishment of this unit until the end of 1993 I was with the 312th Motorised Brigade throughout all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, during this period of time, from the establishment of the 312th Motorised Brigade until the end of 1993, did you hold any type of rank or any position whereby you had soldiers under your command?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: At the very beginning, I was one of the crew of the howitzer. A few months later when we managed to train the second crew and we had two crews, then we established the command platoon of our detachment and two crews on the howitzer. So at one point in time I held the position of the deputy commander of the platoon, of the 105-millimetre howitzer platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall approximately when that was that you assumed this position as deputy commander of the platoon?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what the date was, but I believe that this was sometime in either December or January. December 1992 or January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again referring to the period from the formation of the brigade through the end of 1993, were you at the location at Kaurske Ravni at those times when you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. When the 312th Motorised Brigade was established, I was constantly and exclusively there. This is where I served in the army. This was my position. Kaurske Ravni was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So when you say exclusively there, I just want to understand that at no point in time during 1993 were you involved in combat operations or activities anywhere other than Kaurske Ravni?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: That's correct. During that period of time, we were mostly deployed on Kaurske Ravni. This is where our artillery piece was, and this was our fire position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And throughout this period, again from the formation of the brigade through the end of 1993, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I was living in the settlement of Luka Zagradje. I've already mentioned that. And I've already said that the distance between my village and Mehurici is about two kilometres. Mehurici, in local terms, is a somewhat bigger settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've mentioned it was somewhat bigger in local terms. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the approximate number of people who lived in Mehurici in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Mehurici had about a thousand inhabitants. At that time, the population moved a lot. It is very difficult for me to say exactly how many people there were. A lot of refugees arrived from various parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they would find accommodation in that area. However, when we're talking about the locals who, mind you, also left the area in large numbers, many left with their families and settled abroad. Everybody who had the opportunity to do so did that. But let me say that there were about a thousand or so inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many people lived in Luka Zagradje in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: In 1993, Luka Zagradje had about five or -- 15 or 16 houses, which means that there could have been approximately -- well, let's say there was an average of five to six people inhabiting one of the -- one house. Again, a lot of people arrived after having been expelled from certain parts of Travnik, Vitez, or -- or Jajce, Skender Vakuf, Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, what is the difference or can you tell us the relationship between Luka Zagradje and the village of Zagradje?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The village of Zagradje is an old settlement on the slope of this hill that goes up to Kaurske Ravni. It's a large village which has about 800 inhabitants. Luka, however, is a new settlement which was organised around the school in the 60s. People started building their houses there and moving in. This new settlement, Luka, is in the valley by the river. Zagradje is on a bit more elevated level, on the slope of this hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, from the village or town of Zagradje, would like a be to the north, south, east, west?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Luka is -- was built on the terrain connecting Zagradje and the river valley, and the distance would be about half a kilometre from the very beginning of Zagradje village. And the direction is south-east. Luka is south-east to the village of Zagradje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, during the period from the formation of the brigade through the end of 1993, how frequently were you in the town of Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: When I was free, when I was on leave, that's when I would go to Mehurici. I had a lot of friends down there, and we would gather there in a restaurant owned by a good friend of mine. We would exchange views. We would meet there. We would gather there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I understand that more than a decade later it's hard to perhaps recall, but would you have been there during this period from 1992 through 1993? Would you have been there once a week, once a month, every other month, every couple of days? Roughly how frequently would you be in Mehurici during this period?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: My shifts lasted ten to 12 days. So at least once during that time interval I would go down to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again during the period from the formation of the brigade through the end of 1993, were you at any point in time in Travnik and, if so, approximately how many times?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I went to Travnik rarely, especially when the roads were blocked leading from Mehurici to Travnik via the Bila valley. In the first half of 1993, I went to Travnik very rarely. There was a time when I wouldn't go to Travnik for a few months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return now to your platoon that you were the deputy commander of. Can you tell us which battalion your platoon was part of?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Our platoon did not belong to any battalion. The 312th Motorised Brigade had battalions, but they also had the artillery part of the unit which was called Mad [as interpreted] at the beginning, and later on the Had [as interpreted] Battalion, the howitzer division. This is what the situation was like at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So, sir, during this period from the formation of the brigade through the end of 1993, to whom did you report as the deputy commander? I assume you reported to the platoon commander.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To whom did the platoon commander report?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I was reporting to the platoon commander, and the platoon commander reported to the commander of the howitzer division who resided in Travnik, and that is where he stayed most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to the issue that you discussed with the Defence concerning the arrival of the foreigners whom you described as Arabic or you initially called them Arabs. You told us that they began arriving in the Mehurici area in the summer of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Well, yes. I personally noticed their presence in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, by the summer of 1992, would you describe the situation in Bosnia as being a wartime situation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Certainly. The BiH army was in conflict with the Serbian side. This was a fully-blown conflict. And the situation with the Croatian Defence Council deteriorated by the day, so that towards the end of 1992, we experienced the initial conflicts in the area of Central Bosnia involving the HVO and the BiH army. This occurred, for example, in the area of Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if because of the wartime situation, particularly by the end of 1992 in Central Bosnia, was the security situation tense?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. Once the conflicts escalated in October and November 1992 in the area of Novi Travnik, conflict -- the conflicts involving the BH army and the HVO, the situation, the security situation, was really very tense in the whole area and deteriorated rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I ask you this question, sir, because it would seem that the presence of these foreigners, that is, outsiders, people who were not from the town of Mehurici, did that raise any security concerns in terms of who these people were in light of the increased security situation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Certainly. We wondered where these people came from and how come they were not incorporated into BiH army units. This was an open issue. This is something that we pondered upon quite a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say you wondered why they were not incorporated into BiH army units, is that because these people were primarily fighting with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: We just asked ourselves -- and this was something that was a bit illogical, that foreigners were active in that area, and they were not part of the regular units. They simply evaded that. And we had the impression that they were simply avoiding that. They did not want to become part of the regular forces. They did not want anybody to have command over them. They seemed to be a certain group which did not wish to have a command, which did not accept a command. They acted on their own and moved on their own. They simply did not wish to join the forces which were under the command which existed in that area. At least that is my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I don't have any particular reason to think that. I don't have any knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say the foreigners were active in that area, what do you mean by "active"? Were they involved in combat?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: From what I could see, they did not participate in combat very often. They spent most of the time in that camp of theirs, as they called it. And at the same time, they also would go to different areas where they were conducting their own exercises. They would go and come back. They were constantly moving between the camp and some other areas, but for the most part they didn't participate directly in -- in the operations, and they were not part of the existing units in that area that belonged to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you said that they did not participate in combat very often, and for the most part they didn't participate directly in the operations. Are you aware from firsthand knowledge of situations where they did participate in combat operations with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: In our area of responsibility in this sector towards the Serbian forces, I am aware that they did come out into the field on a couple of occasions, but they would also withdraw without being accountable to anybody. They would just simply come and then they would say that they were surveying the terrain. That's what they would say. They simply did not want to take upon themselves an area of responsibility and hold it. Mostly they operated as freelancers, if I may put it that way. They would be in a certain area for a certain period at their own discretion, and then they would leave when they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, would it be correct to say that one of the distinguishing characteristics of a motorised brigade, in general terms, was that such a brigade would have a large number of vehicles to transport its troops with?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Motorised brigades, by establishment, are composed in such a way that they have strong logistics aspect, and they have everything that they are supposed to have in the composition of the brigade. In this case, our brigade did not really meet these requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: However, sir, you did tell us that the Arabs or what you later called Mujahedin in Mehurici or in the Mehurici area had some vehicles.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. They were recognisable because they had these Toyotas. These were open vehicles, and they would often stand on the flatbed of these vehicles. That was the main distinguishing characteristic that I was able to see when we're talking about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you a few more questions about the vehicles in a moment, but let first ask you: In the last six months, in the last half of 1992, how many Mujahedin were present in the Mehurici area? A rough approximation, if you can inform us of that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I already mentioned that it was very difficult to estimate how many of them there were because they were completely separated and isolated in that camp. And also, when they moved, they didn't walk very often. They would move in the vehicles. So it was very difficult to make a realistic estimate. But in conversations with some of my friends, we came to the conclusion that maybe there were about 100 of them. That was the general impression. Because it was really impossible to make a specific number, because it was really impossible to enter their camp for others, or for anyone except for those who had joined them and who had agreed to work with then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During 1993, did the number of the Mujahedin remain at about 100, or did it increase, or did it decrease?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: This is a difficult question. First of all because I didn't have the opportunity to monitor such changes. But I could say that in the second half of 1993, it became obvious that there were more of them. And it was also obvious that a certain number of the local population had joined them, meaning the people from these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that the number of the Mujahedin, including the local Bosniaks who joined them, the number of these people increased as the conflict with the HVO intensified during 1993?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: In that context, perhaps in a way you could notice something. The most important thing was that, for example, if you were following their presence, their numbers, these were mostly people who were not easy to identify because of the way they looked, because -- because of the way they looked, the clothes that they wore. So it's a little bit difficult to gain a true picture of their true number, the actual number of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that when they -- at the beginning they mostly wore traditional clothes, and then you said on page 13 that later they wore uniforms. What kind of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: They wore these uniforms, military uniforms, which they bought from somewhere. I don't know where. But it's a fact that we knew that they had certain financial means, and by calling and appealing to a certain number of people who had joined them, it was clear -- well, I have to tell you right away that these uniforms were not all the same. They had different uniforms that we could distinguish, ranging from members of some other armies in Europe. How they acquired these uniforms, I really have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return, sir, to the issue of the vehicles. You told us that they had rather characteristic flatbed Toyota vehicles. Do you recall approximately how many such vehicles they had?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I really couldn't say because these vehicles were the same. They all looked the same, so it was difficult to tell them apart. They were white, and it was difficult to distinguish whether we saw one today or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. earlier or which one was new. I can perhaps say that in that time period in that area, they had about ten such vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the vehicles have any type of markings or do you remember what type of licence plates the vehicles had?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I think that most of the vehicles didn't have any licence plates, the ones that were driving around in that area in Mehurici. I don't know whether vehicles used in some other areas had licence plates, but the ones in that area didn't have any markings or licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many people could be transported in each of these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: The open part in the back could fit about ten, eight to ten of them. That's where they would stand. And at least when they would pass through the settlements they would be standing in the back of the vehicles usually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How frequently did you see these Mujahedin travelling in these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN RIBO
utterances.text: I already mentioned before. They mostly moved around in these vehicles. They walked on foot through the settlements very, very rarely. They would most often move around in these vehicles. At that time, I didn't have any opportunity to see them walking in a column or anything like that.
